Hi all,
I have a new result in additive combinatorics with a Lean 4 proof:
η(C_p³) ≥ 8(p−1)+1 for every odd prime p.
This improves Harborth's classical bound of 7(p−1)+1. The construction is eight explicit nonzero vectors in 𝔽_p³, each taken with multiplicity p−1. The proof that no zero-sum of length ≤ p exists reduces to a single integer inequality on the kernel of the 3×8 matrix, established by case analysis on wrap counts and a parity obstruction in the hardest case (the same 2T = p contradiction Elsholtz used for the s-constant).
What Lean actually proves: min_lift_weight — that pN − S₄ ≥ p+1 for every nonzero parameter vector, working entirely in ℤ with explicit bounds. No sorry. 541 lines. The case splits are handled by omega/linarith, with omega closing the parity case cleanly.
What Lean doesn't yet prove: The kernel parametrization step — that every zero-sum of S corresponds to such a parameter vector. That argument is in the paper and is mathematically clean, but not yet formalized. Closing that gap is the obvious next step and I'd welcome pointers to relevant Mathlib infrastructure.
Repo: https://github.com/requitefahrenheit/davenport-eta-cp3
(includes the paper PDF with full proof)
I do additive combinatorics and I have no idea what "η(C_p³)" is. Mind explaining?

Yaël Dillies said:

I do additive combinatorics and I have no idea what "η(C_p³)" is. Mind explaining?

Explained in repo readme:

Here η(G) is the smallest integer ℓ such that every sequence of ℓ elements in G contains a zero-sum subsequence of length at most exp(G).

η(G) is the smallest ℓ such that every sequence of ℓ elements in G contains a zero-sum subsequence of length ≤ exp(G). For G = C_p³ this means zero-sums of length ≤ p. We prove η(C_p³) ≥ 8(p−1)+1 by exhibiting eight explicit nonzero vectors in 𝔽_p³ — one more than Harborth's binary cube construction. The key is a parity obstruction: the hardest case forces 2T = p, which is impossible since p is odd. Happy to answer any questions.
